name: United States
headline: The dollar, the technology, and the depth of the markets.
summary: Born out of a revolution against British taxation, the world's largest economy was built on a vast home market, a business-law framework friendly to capital, and the privilege of the dollar. Today its risk is less insolvency than political polarization, the weight of debt, and dependence on a handful of technology giants.

history.title: Independence
history.text: Thirteen colonies break away from London. The 1787 Constitution creates a common market, a federal currency, and a legal framework that protects property.

history.title: End of the Civil War
history.text: The Union's victory accelerates the industrialization of the North. The country becomes a continental manufacturing power.

history.title: Crash and New Deal
history.text: The crisis exposes the dangers of lightly regulated finance. Roosevelt creates the SEC, unemployment insurance, and public works: the state becomes a stabilizer.

history.title: Bretton Woods
history.text: The dollar becomes the world's reserve currency, convertible into gold. The United States organizes the IMF, the World Bank, and global trade.

history.title: End of gold convertibility
history.text: Nixon closes the gold window. The dollar floats, yet stays dominant thanks to the depth of the Treasury market and to oil priced in dollars.

history.title: Financial crisis and QE
history.text: Lehman's collapse leads to massive Fed asset purchases. Monetary policy becomes a central tool for managing the cycle.

history.title: Inflation, rates, and AI
history.text: The Fed raises rates sharply to break inflation. The economy holds up, carried by employment and investment in artificial intelligence.

institutions.executive: President elected for 4 years, strict separation of powers
institutions.legislature: Bicameral Congress: Senate and House of Representatives
institutions.currency: US dollar (USD), the world's reserve currency
institutions.law: Common law, state-level jurisdictions, strong contractual protection
institutions.fact: The US bond market is the most liquid in the world: it sets the global price of risk.

allies.name: European Union
allies.note: Trade partner, sometimes a rival regulator.

rivals.name: Russia
rivals.note: Geopolitical opposition, sanctions, and arms control.

dependencies.name: China
dependencies.note: Supply chains, rare earths, and consumer goods.

dependencies.name: Taiwan
dependencies.note: Advanced semiconductors: a strategic point of fragility.

dependencies.name: Canada / Mexico
dependencies.note: Trade integrated by the USMCA, plus energy and autos.

gdp_growth.note: Household consumption and technology investment take over from a very expansionary fiscal policy.

inflation.note: Inflation is slowing but still above the 2% target. Services and housing are the last stubborn spots.

debt_gdp.note: Federal debt is high but financed in the reserve currency. The real risk is political: the cost of interest rates.

policy_rate.note: The Fed is easing gradually after the 2023 peak. A positive real rate leaves margin if inflation surprises.

unemployment.note: The labor market remains solid, which supports consumption and delays recession risk.

reserves.note: Reserves matter less for an issuer of the reserve currency: dollar liquidity is the shock absorber.

rating.note: The rating remains very high, despite fiscal strains and congressional gridlock.

cds.note: The market prices low political and fiscal risk over the short run. US CDS serve as the global benchmark.

equity_index.note: Performance is concentrated in tech mega-caps: market breadth is the point to watch.

currency.name: US dollar
currency.note: The dollar remains the safe haven and the dominant invoicing currency. Its strength weighs on countries indebted in dollars.

strengths: Unmatched depth of capital markets and the dollar's status.
Technology ecosystem, universities, and innovation capacity.
Flexible labor market and demographics more dynamic than Europe's.
risks: Political polarization and the risk of fiscal gridlock.
High federal debt in a higher-rate regime.
Market concentration and dependence on technology giants.
opportunities: Investment in AI, semiconductors, and energy.
Partial re-industrialization supported by public subsidies.
Unmatched access to markets for exporters.

quiz.question: Who decides US monetary policy?
quiz.explanation: The Fed is independent of political power. It sets rates to pursue full employment and price stability, even though the Treasury manages the debt.
